paper_title: DISCO: Distributed Long Context Scaling with Grounding-Reasoning Disaggregation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While Large Language Models (LLMs) advertise million-token context windows, reasoning quality often collapses as inputs grow -- a phenomenon termed context rot. This failure stems from a structural entanglement in monolithic architectures, where the massive search burden of contextual grounding exhausts the representational capacity needed for complex reasoning. To resolve this, we propose Grounding-Reasoning Disaggregation via DIStributed long COntext scaling (DISCO). Inspired by distributed computing frameworks like Apache Spark, DISCO partitions long context across a fleet of Worker LLMs dedicated exclusively to parallel, localized grounding. A central Driver LLM, trained via Reinforcement Learning (GRPO) to optimize planning, orchestrates execution by dynamically mapping queries into atomic extraction tasks and reducing the gathered evidence to synthesize a final answer. By isolating reasoning from raw context noise, DISCO effectively eliminates context rot. On RULER-QA (1M tokens), it maintains 78.4% accuracy where standard baselines collapse. Furthermore, it outperforms full-context models by up to 9.8 points on LongBench v2 and matches frontier models like Gemini-3-Pro-Preview while reducing inference costs by over 80%, establishing a highly efficient paradigm for robust long-context inference.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly advertise context windows spanning millions of tokens (OpenAI, 2023; Huang and Yang, 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Yet, even well within nominal limits, reasoning quality frequently collapses as input growsa phenomenon termed context *Work done during an internship at Adobe Research. Corresponding authors. 1 rot (Hsieh et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2025). Consequently, the effective context window of LLMs remains severely limited (Modarressi et al., 2025), hampering their reliability in real-world applications. We argue that context rot stems from fundamental structural asymmetry between two distinct cognitive phases: contextual grounding (identifying relevant facts) and reasoning (synthesizing those facts into an answer). As input length increases, grounding becomes massive search problem that scales proportionally with the text, while the core reasoning task typically remains constant in complexity regardless of the haystacks size. In monolithic Transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017), however, these two processes are irreversibly entangled. Attention heads forced to locate scattered needles across millions of tokens exhaust their representational bandwidth, leaving insufficient residual capacity for multi-hop reasoning. Existing approaches struggle to resolve this entanglement. Retrieval pipelines and agentic memory systems (Chhikara et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) separate retrieval from reasoning, but delegate grounding to shallow mechanisms (e.g., embeddings, BM25) that frequently miss implicitly relevant evidence. Conversely, sequential multi-agent workflows (Zhang et al., 2024b; Qian et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024) apply full LLM-grade understanding to each chunk, but process them seriallyincurring linear latency and fragile cross-step state management that degrades over multiple hops. Ultimately, these paradigms fail to simultaneously achieve deep, parallelizable grounding that is structurally isolated and precise reasoning paths. Experimental results demonstrate that DISCO effectively eliminates context rot: on RULER-QA (1M tokens), DISCO with Qwen3-8B (Qwen, 2025) maintains 78.4% accuracy while standard retrieval baselines collapse to 10.9%. On reasoning-intensive benchmarks, it outperforms Full Long Context baselines by up to 9.8 points (Qwen3-14B) on LongBench v2 (Long subset), with RL tuning further amplifying gains. Crucially, DISCO enables economic scaling: it matches the performance of frontier models like Gemini-3-Pro-Preview while reducing inference costs by over 80%, establishing new paradigm for efficient, high-fidelity long-context inference.

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: We introduce DISCO, distributed inference framework that reframes long-context processing as data-parallel computing problem. Departing from the monolithic paradigmwhere single transient attention mechanism manages millions of tokenswe treat the context as persistent, distributed data. In this section, we derive the theoretical motivation for decoupling contextual grounding from reasoning (2.1), propose distributed architecture to approximate the grounding objective (2.2), formalize the inference process as dynamic Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) (2.3), and describe the iterative orchestration between Driver and Workers (2.4). Finally, we detail the optimization of the Driver via Reinforcement Learning (2.5).

sections.title: 2.1 The Grounding-Reasoning Interference
sections.content: Let long-context task be defined by massive context sequence = (x1, . . . , xL) of length L, query q, and target response y. Standard LLMs with parameters θ model the conditional probability Pθ(y x, q) monolithically. Intuitively, as increases, the relevant information for becomes sparsely distributed across x. Consequently, the cognitive process implicitly bifurcates into two distinct stages: contextual grounding (identifying relevant evidence) and reasoning (synthesizing the answer from that evidence). We formalize this by introducing latent variable z, representing the set of discrete evidence artifacts (facts, snippets, or logical predicates) hidden within x. The generation probability factorizes from reasoning.1 To scale robustly toward millions of tokens, we propose structural paradigm shift: GroundingReasoning Disaggregation. The core principle is to decouple these two phases entirely, ensuring that complex reasoning is conducted exclusively over highly refined subset of facts extracted during an independent, parallelized grounding stage. By isolating the heavy lifting of information retrieval from the cognitive load of synthesis, we protect the models reasoning capabilities from being overwhelmed by scale. To realize this disaggregation, we introduce DIStributed long COntext scaling (DISCO), an architecture directly inspired by distributed computing frameworks like Apache Spark (Zaharia et al., 2010, 2016). Conceptually, an LLMs limited effective context window is analogous to the operational memory (RAM) of single compute node. When data exceeds this capacity, systems like Spark do not build larger nodes; instead, they schedule multiple nodes to process data shards in parallel. Adopting this metaphor, DISCO partitions the massive context into shards distributed across fleet of logical Worker LLMs. Each Worker persistently holds its own shard to conduct local, high-fidelity grounding. These Workers are orchestrated by central Driver LLM, which functions as high-level planner and synthesizer. Inspired by directed acyclic graph (DAG) execution models, the Driver decomposes complex user queries into parallelizable atomic actions. Rather than relying on rigid linear processing, the system maps information-intensive extraction tasks across the Workers to gather facts independently from their local shards, and subsequently reduces these aggregated insights through global reasoning pass by the Driver to synthesize the final answer. DISCO operates dynamically, iteratively replanning the DAG until sufficient evidence is gathered. This separation enables pure inference-time scaling: as context grows, we scale Map actions; as reasoning complexity increases, we scale Widedependency actions. Furthermore, DISCO provides native environment for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We employ Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) to train the Driver LLM, incentivizing optimal execution plans 1Alternative approaches like memory-augmented architectures (Behrouz et al., 2024) internalize long-range retention but currently demand prohibitive pre-training from scratch, leaving generalization underexplored. 2 as: Pθ(y x, q) = (cid:88) Pθ(y z, q) (cid:124) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) Reasoning Pθ(z x, q) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) (cid:124) Grounding .2 (1) In monolithic architectures, single set of parameters θ within single attention window attempts to approximate both terms simultaneously. This coupling creates critical bottleneck: as grows, the complexity of the grounding term PΘ(z x, q) degrades rapidly due to architectural limitations (e.g., context rot and the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon), where attention mechanisms fail to distinguish signal from noise. Consequently, the task fails not due to lack of reasoning capability, but due to collapse in the evidences grounding. 2.2 DISCO: Distributed Long Context Scaling Paradigm Contextual grounding over massive sequences becomes the primary bottleneck in long-context scaling. To circumvent the limitations of directly modeling the full sequence, we introduce Distributed Context Scaling (DISCO), paradigm that structurally decouples contextual grounding via context partitioning. We split the massive context into disjoint shards {x(k)}K k=1, ensuring that each shard falls comfortably within the high-fidelity window of standard LLM. sections.title: Graphs
sections.content: While the distributed architecture described in 2.2 enables massive parallelization, it introduces capability gap: lightweight Workers (θW ) often lack the reasoning depth required to handle complex, multi-hop queries directly. To bridge this gap, we draw inspiration from distributed computing systems (e.g., Apache Spark) and utilize the Driver θD as central planner. The Driver decomposes the user query into Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) = (V, E), where nodes represent executable actions and edges denote data dependencies. To accommodate the disparate capabilities of the models, we classify nodes into two distinct functional types: 1. Narrow Actions (Map: Atomic Extraction). Narrow actions rely exclusively on local context and are executed by Workers. To mitigate the risk of reasoning failure in smaller models, we restrict these actions to atomic, entity-centric extraction. sections.title: Refinement
sections.content: The optimal computation topology for query is rarely known priori. DISCO therefore employs an online planning process formalized as multistage loop: the Driver iteratively constructs, executes, and evaluates DAGs until the query is resolved. 1. Planning Phase (DAG Construction). At stage t, the Driver θD acts as Planner, conditioning on query and the execution history to generate DAG Gt. The graph mixes Narrow nodes (shardlevel probes) and intermediate Wide nodes (partial synthesis), structured so that the terminal node Wide Action representing itselfreceives the most refined information flow. 2. Execution Phase (Evidence Pooling). The system executes Gt in topological order, maintaining stage-specific evidence pool Zt. Narrow Actions are dispatched to Workers θW , which scan their shards in parallel and materialize atomic facts into Zt. Wide Actions are then processed by the Driver as Reducer: it retrieves dependent outputs 4 from Zt, performs logical synthesis, and writes results back into the pool. vides immediate feedback at each step to ensure executability. 3. Evaluation and Refinement. Upon DAG the Driver examines the terminal completion, nodes output ˆyt. If the evidence suffices to answer with high confidence, the process terminates. Otherwise, the Driver rejects the output and advances to stage + 1, where it leverages Zt to generate refined graph Gt+1 targeting the identified information gaps. 2.5 Optimizing the Driver via Reinforcement Learning Since optimal intermediate DAG structures lack ground truth supervision, we treat the Driver as an agent and optimize it using Reinforcement Learning. We employ Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) to refine the Drivers policy. Unlike standard single-turn generation, complete inference episode in DISCO produces trajectory τ consisting of multiple discrete sequences τ = (s1, . . . , sT ), corresponding to the iterative planning steps and the final reasoning output. We optimize the policy against composite reward function: = λaRacc + λeRevd + λfRfmt. (7) The Accuracy Reward Racc {0, 1} evaluates the correctness of the final response against the ground truth. To ensure high-fidelity grounding, we introduce an Evidence Reward Revd {0, 1}, which employs judge model to verify that is logically derived strictly from the accumulated evidence Z. This explicitly penalizes answers that are factually correct relative to external knowledge but unsupported by the retrieved context (hallucinations). Finally, to enforce structural validity, the Format Reward Rfmt {1, 0} applies penalty if the generated DAG contains syntax errors or invalid dependencies, and is 0 otherwise. critical challenge in this multi-turn setting is credit assignment, as task-level utility is only observable at the terminal state. Consequently, following Yu et al. (2025), we broadcast the terminal rewards (Racc and Revd) to all intermediate sequences st within the trajectory. sections.title: 3 Experimental Setup
sections.content: 3.1 Evaluation Protocol Baselines. We compare DISCO against representative methods covering direct processing, retrieval, and agentic workflows: (1) Naive LongContext, where the full context is fed directly into the models window to assess native performance and degradation; (2) Standard RAG, implementing dense retrieval pipeline using Qwen3Embedding-4B to fetch the top-16 chunks (256 tokens each) based on cosine similarity; (3) Chainof-Agents (CoA) (Zhang et al., 2024b), which processes partitioned context sequentially, passing summarized information between worker agents; (4) LLMMapReduce (Zhou et al., 2024), divide-and-conquer approach employing parallel evidence extraction followed by single aggregation step; (5) Recursive Language Model (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025), an interactive system where the model recursively queries the text environment to gather information. (See more details in A.2) Benchmarks. We assess performance across three benchmarks: (1) LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2024), comprehensive multi-choice suite evaluating contexts ranging from 8K to 2M tokens. We evaluate on the Medium (32K-128K) and Long (>128K) subsets. (2) RULER-QA (Hsieh et al., 2024), synthetic benchmark testing multi-hop reasoning over arbitrary context length. We focus on this QA task with the lengths of 256K, 512K, and 1M tokens. (3) Bench (Zhang et al., 2024a). We evaluate all models on two tasks in this benchmark: long-book question answering (En.QA), and multichoice question-answering (En.MC). The average evaluation length is from 150K to 200K. Models and Implementation. We evaluate DISCO and the state-of-the-art baselines using three backbone LLMs: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview. For open-weight models, we utilize SGLang (Zheng et al., 2023) for efficient inference, with context length extended to 128K by YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) across all baselines. In DISCO, we use the Qwen3-4B-Instruct2507 as the Worker LLM across evaluations except specifically mentioned. We set the context shard size of each worker as 4096 and maximum replanning stages as 10. 5 Table 1: Evaluation results of models on long-context benchmarks. Training Data Construction. We construct our training set using the MuSiQue dataset (Trivedi et al., 2021) to ensure high reasoning complexity. To synthesize the massive contexts required to test distributed scaling (16K512K tokens), we developed Recursive Context Augmentation pipeline. Leveraging Qwen3-235B-A22B-Think2507, we identify entity mentions within supporting claims and recursively replace them with the full content of their linked Wikipedia pages (Pe). This transformation follows the schema . . . [e] . . . . . . [CONTENT(Pe)] . . . , effectively embedding sparse retrieval targets within extensive unstructured text. We apply consistency filter to prune samples where expansion introduces logical contradictions, yielding 4.5k high-fidelity samples. More details are listed in A.3. Training Setup. We train two models, Qwen38B (thinking) and Qwen3-14B (thinking), employing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024). Training proceeds for 2 epochs on the curated 4.5K dataset using the AdamW optimizer with constant learning rate of 1e6 and 5-step linear warmup. During the rollout phase, we set global batch size of 256 and sample = 8 trajectories per prompt, enforcing maximum context window of 24K tokens and generation limit of 16K tokens. We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the Worker LLM (shard size=4096) during training. We utilize Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 as the judge model for reward computation. The weighting coefficients for the composite reward function (Eq. (7)) are set to λacc = 1.0 and λfmt = λevd = 0.5.

sections.title: 4.1 Main Results
sections.content: We validate DISCO on LongBench v2, RULERQA, and Bench, using Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Gemini-3-Pro. The results confirm the effectiveness of our three core architectural pillars: distributed grounding, decoupled reasoning, and economic scalability. Distributed Partitioning Ensures Robust Grounding at Scale. In Table 1, our results demonstrate that by utilizing distributed context partitioning, DISCO achieves superior contextual grounding compared to all baselines, maintaining robustness even up to the 1M token scale. This is strikingly evident on RULER-QA: while RAG fails to retrieve relevant segments from the massive 6 Figure 2: Thinking Mode accuracy gains on LongBench v2. DISCO amplifies the benefit of extended reasoning (e.g., +13.5 vs. +5.6 for Qwen3-14B) by freeing the Driver from grounding overhead. search spacecollapsing to 10.9% accuracy with Qwen3-8BDISCO sustains 78.4%. Unlike methods that degrade with length, our distributed architecture renders grounding performance invariant to the total context size. By unshackling the system from the bottlenecks of heuristic retrieval and static windowing, DISCO outperforms the strongest baseline (LLMMapReduce) by 6%, proving that dynamic partitioning is essential for high recall in the million-token regime. Decoupling and Replanning Unleash Reasoning Potential. We attribute the superior performance of DISCO to the Drivers dynamic DAG planning, which structurally decouples grounding (Workers) from reasoning (Driver). Unlike LLMMapReducewhich relies on rigid, single-pass scan where workers must handle full query complexityDISCO operates iteratively: the Driver decomposes multi-hop queries into atomic retrieval steps (Narrow Actions) and synthesizes intermediate results (Wide Actions), dynamically re-planning based on feedback. On LongBench v2, DISCO (Qwen3-14B) achieves 9.8 point gain over Full Long Context (48.7% vs 38.9%) and substantially outperforms LLMMapReduce (33.7%). This decoupling also amplifies intrinsic reasoning capacity. As shown in Figure 2, enabling Thinking Mode under Full Long Context yields modest gains (+0.9 for 8B, +5.6 for 14B), as extended reasoning is largely consumed by grounding through noisy context. DISCO magnifies these gains to +5.5 and +13.5 respectivelysince Workers have Figure 3: The accuracy and evaluation costs on LongBench v2 (Long) using Gemini-3-Pro as the Driver. DISCO matches the performance of full context processing while reducing financial cost by over 80%. Figure 4: Impact of Worker model scale on accuracy and planning efficiency. While larger Workers yield only marginal accuracy gains, they significantly reduce the number of planning stages required by the Driver to converge. already distilled compact evidence, the Drivers thinking budget is spent entirely on reasoning. Architecture Decouples Cost from Scale. Finally, DISCO proves effective at enabling the economic deployment of frontier-class reasoning on massive context. By offloading token-intensive scanning to lightweight Workers, we decouple the cost of reading from the cost of thinking. As shown in Figure 3 with Gemini-3-Pro, DISCO retains the reasoning parity of the Full Context baseline (71.3% vs. 72.2%) while slashing evaluation costs by 6.2 ($126.7 $20.4). This validates DISCO as scalable wrapper that allows superior LLMs to process million-token contexts without the prohibitive quadratic costs of standard attention. 4.

sections.title: Impact of Reward Design
sections.content: To validate our composite reward function (Eq. 7), we ablate the Evidence (Revd) and Format (Rfmt) rewards on Qwen3-8B  (Table 2)  . Planning Efficiency (Revd). Removing Revd reduces accuracy and spikes execution length. Without penalties for ungrounded hallucinations, the Driver fails to distinguish valid evidence from noise, leading to partially supported answers, frequent self-evaluation rejections, and costly replanning loops. Structural Stability (Rfmt). Omitting Rfmt yields the lowest accuracy and highest latency. Without structural penalties enforcing schema compliance, the Driver frequently generates syntactically invalid DAGs. This triggers automatic retries, wasting computational cycles on exception handling rather than task progression. 4.

sections.title: Inference Efficiency and Scalability
sections.content: We evaluate inference latency on the RULERQA benchmark across context lengths of 256K to 1M under fixed iso-compute budget of 8H100 GPUs. Baselines deploy monolithic Qwen3-14B (TP=8), whereas DISCO adopts heterogeneous strategy, allocating 4 GPUs to Driver (Qwen3-14B) and 4 to parallel Workers (Qwen3-4B). As shown in Figure 5, DISCO significantly outperforms agentic baselines (CoA, LLMMapReduce), maintain8 Figure 5: End-to-end latency on RULER-QA under an iso-compute budget (8H100). DISCO maintains nearconstant latency as context scales to 1M tokens. ing near-flat latency profile while baselines exhibit steep linear growth. By offloading the highvolume token processing to efficient Workers, we circumvent the bottleneck of processing massive sequences with large parameters. Furthermore, the RL-tuned variant achieves the highest efficiency by optimizing planning paths to minimize execution steps. These results demonstrate the superior long-context scaling potential of DISCO.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Distributed Computing Paradigms. The management of massive datasets was revolutionized by MapReduce (Dean et al., 2004) and Hadoop (Shvachko et al., 2010), which introduced paradigm of moving computation to data rather than transferring data to compute nodes. Apache Spark further advanced this by introducing Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs) and Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) scheduling, enabling efficient in-memory iterative processing. These systems decompose complex queries into Map (parallel processing) and Reduce (aggregation) operations. Our work adapts these classical distributed primitives to the domain of LLMs, treating long context as distributed data that requires orchestrated, parallel processing rather than monolithic ingestion. Long-Context Processing in LLMs. Current approaches to handling extensive context generally fall into three categories: (1) Architectural Extrapolation. primary line of research focuses on extending the context window of single models via length extrapolation strategies (Chen et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2023; An et al., 2024) or memory-augmented architectures (Behrouz et al., 2024, 2025) empowered by test-time training (Tandon et al., 2025). While these methods expand the nominal window size, they frequently suffer from context rot, where reasoning capabilities degrade significantly as input length increases (Hong et al., 2025; Modarressi et al., 2025). Furthermore, training memory modules from scratch poses generalization challenges that remain underexplored. (2) Retrieval and Agentic Memory. To bypass architectural limits, systems rely on RAG or, more recently, agentic memory frameworks that selectively compress, edit, and retrieve context (Chhikara et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025). While scalable, these select-based pipelines face fundamental retrieval bottleneck: they optimize for local semantic similarity, often discarding implicitly pertinent information required for global reasoning (Hu et al., 2025; Du et al., 2025). Even just-intime mechanisms (Yan et al., 2025) ultimately rely on imperfect recall to recover lost information. (3) Agentic Workflows. Recent works have proposed decomposing long context processing into agent workflows. Chain-of-Agents (Zhang et al., 2024b) and subsequent variants (Qian et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024) process chunks sequentially, passing information in chain. However, this serialization incurs prohibitive latency and suffers from cascading information loss. LLMMapReduce (Zhou et al., 2024) attempts parallel scanning evidences and aggregation using single LLM for each user query, which often lacks the scalability to handle complex, multi-hop reasoning over millions of tokens. While Recursive LMs (Zhang et al., 2025) introduce environment-based interaction for long context, they only remain effective upon massive LLMs (hundreds of billions of parameters) with strong coding capabilities. In contrast, DISCO decouples contextual grounding from reasoning. By adopting distributed system view, we enable smaller Workers to process short chunks in parallel (Map) while central Driver orchestrates high-level logic (Shuffle/Reduce), overcoming the latency of sequential agents and the precision loss of retrieval systems, hence becoming more scalable for long context.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: ing. By partitioning massive contexts across fleet of Worker LLMs orchestrated by central, GRPO-trained Driver, DISCO effectively eliminates context rot, maintaining robust fidelity up to one million tokens where monolithic architectures collapse. Isolating the reasoning engine from raw data noise creates high-signal environment optimized for complex, multi-hop tasks. This disaggregation not only elevates reasoning capabilities but also achieves the accuracy of frontier models at fraction of the inference cost. Ultimately, DISCO signals critical paradigm shift: moving away from passively expanding single-node context windows, and toward building active, distributed systems designed to navigate unbounded information landscapes.

sections.content: A.1 Algorithm A.2 Evaluation Details Baselines. We evaluate all baselines following their official implementations, with the exception of Chain-of-Agents, for which code is unavailable; in this case, we reproduced the method following the papers details. We set the chunk size to 4096 for both Chain-of-Agents and LLMMapReduce. For the Recursive Language Model (RLM), we adopt the official settings with maximum depth of 1 and 30 iterations. We observed that RLM fails to perform effectively with Qwen3-8B/14B. This aligns with the original authors findings that smaller LLMs lack the sufficient coding and planning capabilities required for recursive interaction within REPL environments. For the full long context baseline, we truncate the length within 128K in the middle following LongBench v2 and Bench official settings. Benchmarks. We found that the standard F1 score metric for En.QA is highly unstable due to the diversity of prediction formats. To address this, we employ Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct as an external judge to verify if the prediction semantically matches the ground truth, assigning binary score of 0 or 1. A.3 Training Data Construction We derive our training set from the MuSiQue dataset (Trivedi et al., 2021), selected for its high complexity in multi-hop reasoning. However, the native context length of MuSiQue (comprising limited Wikipedia paragraphs) is insufficient to saturate the capacity of our distributed Worker fleet or test long-context robustness. To address this, we developed Recursive Context Augmentation pipeline to scale the input length from standard baselines to 16K512K tokens. We employ Qwen3-235B-A22B-Think-2507 to traverse the entity links within the original supporting facts. For given claim containing an entity mention that links to an external Wikipedia page Pe, we perform semantic expansion. We define transformation function (C, e, Pe) that rewrites the claim to embed the full content of the external page while maintaining narrative coherence. The 11 Table 3: Comparison of DISCO using Generative Worker versus Dense Retriever baseline. The Driver is Qwen3-14B after our RL training. LongBench v2 Worker Type Medium Long Avg Qwen3-Embedding-4B Qwen3-4B-Instruct 37.2 43.7 39.6 41.9 50.9 47.30 distinct phase transition. In the low-noise regime (p 0.2), the system is highly resilient: accuracy remains stable near 51% with negligible increase in planning steps (4 stages). This indicates the Drivers reasoning is robust to bridge partial information gaps without incurring overhead. However, tipping point occurs at = 0.3: average stages spike sharply (from 4 to 7) as Driver is forced into repeated search loops, causing accuracy to plummet to 33% at = 0.5. This confirms that while DISCO withstands moderate worker failure, excessive information loss eventually exhausts the inference budget (Tmax = 10), leading to termination before convergence. Generative Worker LLM Outperforms Dense Retriever. core premise of DISCO is that contextual grounding requires processing information using generative LLMs, not just matching it. To validate the necessity of generative Worker LLMs, we conducted an ablation study comparing our distributed active processing approach against standard passive retrieval baseline. We replaced the generative Worker (Qwen3-4B-Instruct) with dense retriever of equivalent parameter scale (Qwen3-Embedding-4B). In the baseline setting, instead of executing Map operations, the system retrieves the top-k (where = 16, chunk size = 256) most semantically similar chunks based on the queries from Planner and feeds them directly to the Reducer. Empirical results in Table 3 reveal substantial performance margin: DISCO achieves score of 47.3, significantly outperforming the embedding-based baseline at 39.6 on LongBench v2. This confirms that standard RAG pipelines suffer from semantic gapembedding similarity often fails to capture diverse and task-specific dependencies required for effective grounding. In contrast, the generative Worker acts as dynamic filter, performing inference-time computation to extract implicitly relevant evidence z(k) that static Figure 6: System resilience to information loss (Fact Dropout). Performance remains stable under moderate noise (p 0.2) but degrades sharply as excessive loss forces the Driver into exhaustion loops (p 0.3). expansion follows the template: : . . . [e] . . . . . . [CONTENT(Pe)] . . . (8) Representative Case: Consider claim mentioning location. Original Claim: The event took place in [Paris], spanning three days. Expanded Context: The event took place in [Paris, which is the capital and most populous city of France... (full text of page) ...], spanning three days. This method effectively creates massive context blocks that are semantically linked to the query but dispersed, forcing the model to perform long-range information retrieval rather than local scanning. To ensure data integrity, we apply Consistency Filter. For every expanded sample, we feed the augmented context and the original ground truth reasoning path to Qwen3-235B-A22B-Think-2507. The model filters out any samples where the injected external text introduces factual contradictions or invalidates the original reasoning chain. The final dataset consists of 4.5k samples with length distribution uniformly spread between 16K and 512K tokens. A.4 More Experimental Results Fault Tolerance via Iterative Replanning. To evaluate resilience against extraction failures, we simulate Fact Dropout scenario where fraction [0.0, 0.5] of narrow action outputs are discarded. As shown in Figure 6, DISCO exhibits Table 4: Generalization of DISCO across diverse Driver and Worker model combinations on LongBench v2 (Long). DISCO consistently improves over the FullContext CoT baseline regardless of the driver model family. Driver Worker Score LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct Ministral-8B-Reasoning (Full Context, CoT) 25.90 Ministral-3-8B-Instruct (FP8) 28.70 27.80 Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Full Context, CoT) Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 32.41 37.96 Gemini-3-Pro-Preview Ministral-3-8B-Instruct (FP8) 70.37 vector index misses. Generalization across Driver and Worker Families. To verify that the benefits of DISCO are not specific to the Qwen3 model family used in Table 1, we further evaluate diverse DriverWorker pairings on LongBench v2 (Long). As shown in Table 4, the gain pattern is preserved across families: pairing LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct with Ministral3-8B Worker lifts accuracy from 25.9 (Full-Context CoT) to 28.7 (+2.8), and Ministral-8B-Reasoning improves from 32.41 to 37.96 (+5.55) when paired with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 Worker. The Worker family itself is fungibleLLaMA-3.170B with Ministral-3-8B and Qwen3-4B Workers reaches comparable scores (28.7 vs. 27.8) indicating that the Driver only requires atomic factual extraction, not specific model lineage. Finally, Gemini-3-Pro-Preview with Ministral3-8B Worker reaches 70.37, within 1 point of the Qwen3-4B Worker result reported in Figure 3 (71.3). Together, these results corroborate the decoupling thesis: with grounding distributed to lightweight, swappable Workers, the systems reasoning ceiling is dictated by the Driver, while the Worker only needs to be competent extractor. A.5 Case Studies of RL Benefits To complement the quantitative results, we trace representative DISCO trajectories on LongBench v2 (Long) under two Driver configurations: After RL (Qwen3-8B-DISCO, GRPO-tuned) and Before RL (Qwen3-8B base), with Workers held constant so the only variable is the Drivers planning capability. Two qualitative improvements consistently emerge across the 15 sampled trajectories, illustrated by the case boxes below. Atomic, Entity-Specific Query Decomposition. Before RL, the Driver routinely forwards generic, near-verbatim multi-hop queries to Workers, often re-using the same shard key across multiple NARROW transformsdiluting evidence quality and forcing extra replanning rounds. After RL, the Driver decomposes the question into atomic subqueries that each target distinct entity localized in single shard. Across the suite, this learned decomposition reduces the average planning stages to 3.39  (Table 2)  , confirming that the Driver learns to atomize multi-hop queries rather than offloading them wholesale. Case A: Kalamang Language Translation Task. Translate the Kalamang phrase terus ter-nan koyet inier tamu kon misis wis into English. After RL. 317 facts, converged in 1 stage. The Driver issues three NARROWs that partition the phrase into disjoint word-level segments: N1: key=terus ter-nan, query=Extract English translations for terus, ter-nan N2: key=koyet inier tamu, query=Extract English translations for koyet, inier, tamu N3: key=kon misis wis, query=Extract English translations for kon, misis, wis Before RL. 69 facts (4.6 fewer), 1 stage. The Driver reuses one document-level key for all four NARROWs, and one transform pastes the entire user query verbatim into single Worker prompt: N1N3: key=kalamang language (reused), query=Translate koyet / wis / misis N4: query=Translate the phrase terus ter-nan koyet inier tamu kon misis wis key=kalamang language, Observation. The After-RL Driver assigns disjoint, atomic key segments aligned to chunked storage. The Before-RL Driver collapses to one generic key and pastes the entire user query into N4an instruction that no single Worker chunk can satisfy. Case D: Zhuang-to-Chinese Translation Task. Translate the Zhuang sentence Gou sien youq aen hekdiemq into Chinese using provided textbook. After RL. 37 facts, 1 stage. The Driver uses the exact source sentence as the extraction key, directing Workers to the precise location of its translation: N1: key=Gou sien youq aen hekdiemq, query=Find the exact Chinese translation for this Zhuang sentence 13 N2: key=Zhuang vocabulary, query=Extract Chinese meanings for related Zhuang words Before RL. 2 facts (18.5 fewer), 5 stages, forcefinalized. All NARROWs reuse generic topic label that does not match any chunk substring: N1N3: key=Zhuang language translation (reused, topic label, no chunk match) Observation. The After-RL Driver localizes against the unique source sentence; the Before-RL Drivers topic label produces no surface-level matches and the run exhausts Tmax=5 without converging. Well-Formed DAGs and Faster Convergence. RL also stabilizes DAG schema compliance, eliminating the retry storms caused by malformed transforms or unparseable Worker prompts. This is the qualitative root cause of the latency gap reported in Table 2: ablating Rfmt pushes latency from 381 to 499 due to repeated structural retries on rejected DAGs. Case G: Enterprise Survey Analysis (FormatError Collapse) Task. Recommend portfolio strategy from 2023 enterprise survey and 2024 quarterly report. After RL. 3 NARROWs, 224 facts, 0 Worker errors. Before RL. 8 NARROWs, 0 facts, 459 cumulative Worker parse errors. The Drivers malformed queries cause Workers to raise parse exceptions on every shard: N1=63 N2=72 N3=49 N4=65 N6=83 N7=56 N8=35 (errors) N5=36 Observation. The Before-RL Driver suffers complete planning collapse: every Worker invocation fails, no facts are extracted, and the orchestrator force-finalizes with empty context. The After-RL Drivers three wellformed NARROWs achieve full coverage with zero parse failures. Case H: Aggregate Convergence over 15 LongBench v2 (Long) Samples Stages to final answer After RL Before RL 1 (immediate convergence) 23 45 (hit max-stage cap) 15 / 15 0 / 15 0 / 15 7 / 15 2 / 15 6 / 15 Observation. The Before-RL Driver hits the max-stage cap on 40% of cases; the orchestrator must force final answer via <force_final>yes</force_final>. The After-RL Driver converges in single stage on every sample.
